summary:
Pskov Oblast stands under the national framework of Russia, where transgender visitors face severe legal and physical risk. Legal gender recognition and gender-affirming care were banned outright in 2023, when the law prohibiting gender reassignment surgery and legal gender changes to official documents was signed; the Supreme Court has designated the "international LGBT movement" an extremist organisation; and the expanded propaganda law criminalises public expression that, explicitly, "justifies" gender transition. Foreigners who breach these provisions face arrest, up to 15 days' detention and deportation, and national government travel warnings say so directly.

The UK Home Office country policy and information note on sexual orientation and gender identity and expression (June 2025, assessment updated 11 June 2025) is the baseline against which Pskov Oblast is scored, with no deviation recorded for the region. Under that baseline same-sex activity is not criminalised, while same-sex marriage and gender transition are banned and no specific legal protections exist.

Penalties are severe. The 'gay propaganda' statute carries administrative fines, with repeat offences punishable by up to 4 years in prison. The 2023 extremist designation of the International LGBT Movement carries 2 to 6 years for participating and 6 to 10 years for organising. Human Rights Watch (30 June 2025) recorded 101 extremism convictions tied to that designation.

Enforcement volume is documented. Between January 2024 and June 2025 at least 20 people faced criminal charges under the designation, one of whom died by suicide in pretrial detention while courts sentenced two to prison; separately, 81 people across 98 cases were found guilty under article 20.3 of the Code of Administrative Offenses for displaying banned symbols, with participation in the designated movement carrying up to 12 years. Between 2022 and 2024 at least 139 people in Russia were impacted by anti-LGBT+ laws through convictions, detentions and extremism prosecutions.

The Home Office note contains no findings specific to Pskov Oblast or to the Northwestern Federal District, so nothing in the recorded record softens the national baseline for this region.
tangentialFactors:
The US State Department travel advisory for Russia is Level 4, Do Not Travel, and carries warnings written for LGBT travellers; official national government advisories tell LGBT travellers to expect arrest and detention.

Enforcement has expanded in pace as well as reach. Meduza reported on 19 June 2025 that cases under Russia's propaganda laws grew eighteenfold over the preceding decade, and that fines under those statutes brought more than 60 million rubles into the state budget in the two years before. The Guardian documented on 17 January 2024 that within 48 hours of the Supreme Court's extremist ruling, masked police raided LGBTQ-friendly Moscow bars, where roughly 100 patrons at one venue were ordered to face the wall, searched and photographed, and at least two further venues were raided the same night.

Lethal outcomes are on the record. The Associated Press reported in December 2024 that a Russian man detained on extremism-related charges over an LGBTQ+ travel agency was found dead in a pretrial detention facility. The Moscow Times (23 June 2025) reported that arrests, club raids and extremism charges defined LGBTQ+ life in Russia through 2025.

Coercive conversion practices are documented against transgender people: BBC Russian (27 July 2024) followed "Ada", a transgender woman lured by relatives in summer 2021 to a conversion-therapy centre near Novosibirsk, where she was held nine months and forced to take testosterone, pray and perform manual labour before escaping after police responded to a phone she had found.
localsOnly:
Russian citizens and residents are exposed to the domestic enforcement machinery behind these figures. Of the 101 extremism convictions recorded by Human Rights Watch, the administrative track under article 20.3 of the Code of Administrative Offenses alone reached 81 people in 98 cases for displaying banned symbols, while the criminal track produced at least 20 charges between January 2024 and June 2025 with two prison sentences.

The 2022 to 2024 total of at least 139 people impacted by anti-LGBT+ laws covers convictions, detentions and extremism prosecutions, all of them proceedings against people inside the country rather than against travellers.

The UK Home Office country policy and information note affirms that LGBT+ people in Russia, including the autonomous republic of Chechnya, constitute a particular social group under the refugee convention, which sets the assessment standard for UK asylum claims and gives a documented basis for residents who flee.
outOfScopeNotes:
No Pskov Oblast-specific or Northwestern Federal District findings appear in the UK Home Office country policy and information note (June 2025), so the regional score is inherited from the national baseline rather than evidenced locally; whether regional courts have issued article 20.3 or extremism convictions in Pskov Oblast is unresolved and not sourced here.

The inventory does not source the availability or absence of gender-affirming care providers, identity-document offices or shelter facilities within Pskov Oblast, and does not record any regional government statement on LGBT+ policy, so those points remain unresolved rather than negative findings.
